To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the amplification of shear tractions by the presence of cratonic roots increases stress in the elastic lithosphere by at most a small factor, and (2) stress patterns in the lithosphere are sensitive to regional variations in basal tractions but not to local variations.

(1) the presence of a continental root amplifies mantle tractions beneath the craton, (2) this amplification increases elastic stresses by at most 1.5, and (3) the amplification does not produce a stress pattern that correlates to local basal traction variations.

(a) the presence of a cratonic root increases the magnitude of basal tractions by a factor of 1.4-4 compared to a viscosity structure with no cratonic roots, (b) the increase in basal traction beneath a craton increases stress magnitudes within the overlying elastic layer by a factor of at most 1.5, and (c) the increase in stress magnitudes is not correlated to local increases in basal tractions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interaction of the mantle and the lithosphere and its influence on the stress state of the lithosphere.
the interaction between the elastic lithosphere and the viscous mantle.
the role of the mantle in the generation of stress in the lithosphere and the implications for the evolution of the lithosphere.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence of continental roots may increase the magnitude of the stress field in the overlying lithosphere but not in the way we might expect.
the lithospheric elastic stresses are not correlated to the lithospheric mantle basal tractions, which are in turn correlated to the lithosphere thickness and lithospheric mantle viscosity.

, while continental roots can increase mantle tractions beneath the cratons, they do not necessarily increase the stress field in the overlying lithosphere, and that the stress field in a given location can be strongly influenced by the strength of surrounding lithosphere.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the lithospheric elastic stress field is largely insensitive to the presence of continental roots.

the presence of a continental root can locally increase basal tractions by up  to a factor of four, but that the effect on the overlying elastic crust is only a factor of 1.5, and that the stress field is more sensitive to regional average changes in basal tractors than local changes.

the presence of cratons may locally increase basal tractions by as much as 4 times compared to a layered structure, but the resulting increase in elastic stresses in the overlying lithosphere is at most 1.5 times, with a maximum increase of 1.1 times at the craton margins.
The main takeaway from our work is that

stress magnitudes are sensitive to the regional distribution of basal tractions, and that local increases in mantle-litospheric coupling may be insufficient to explain local variations in stress patterns.
the elastic response to basal tractions may be significantly more sensitive to regional variations in mantle viscosity than to the presence of deeply penetrating roots.
, while the lithosphere may be locally weak, it is not necessarily weak everywhere.
